To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) physical training increases the GH response to exercise, but not the response to GHRH, in normally cycling women, (b) the increase in GH response to exercise is greater in older women and in women with low body fat, and (c) the increase in the GH response to physical training is associated with a reduction in the age-related decline of the GH response to a single bout of exercise.

1) the GH response to exercise is blunted with aging and is associated with a reduction in GH secretory burst frequency; and 2) the blunting of the GH response to resistance exercise is attenuated by physical training in older women.

the study of the effect of physical training on the age-related decline of GH secretion during dynamic exercise in normally cycling, healthy women.
understanding the mechanisms by which exercise training affects the secretion of GH and IGF-I.
the effect of physical training on the age-related reduction of growth hormone secretion during exercise in women.

the effects of exercise on the GH-IGF-1 axis are not fully understood, and that the effects of physical activity on GH secretion and IGF-1 production are complex, and depend on the type of exercise, the training status of the subject, the intensity of exercise, and the time of day of the exercise bout.
physical activity and exercise training are effective in improving insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes.
exercise training is beneficial for improving the cardiovascular system in the general population, including those with type 2 diabetes.

the effect of physical exercise on GH secretion is dependent on age and the intensity of exercise.

the effects of exercise on the hypothalamo-pituitary axis are dependent on the type, intensity, and frequency of the exercise.
